claim: The uaDf5 mtDNA deletion mutation is a 3.1-kb deletion that removes part or all of four protein-coding genes and seven tRNAs.
source: To test the role of potential regulatory factors in mtDNA purifying selection, we took advantage of uaDf5, a 3.1-kb mtDNA deletion mutation that removes part or all of four protein-coding genes and seven tRNAs (Figure 1A; Tsang and Lemire, 2002).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by a citation to Tsang and Lemire, 2002, and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: The uaDf5-bearing strain contains a second mtDNA mutation, w47, which is a single base pair insertion in the nduo-4 gene.
source: Comprehensive sequence analysis revealed that, in addition to the large deletion, the strain indeed carries a second mtDNA mutation, w47 (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C). w47 is a single base pair insertion in the nduo-4 gene that causes a frameshift, predicted to result in a truncated NADH dehydrogenase 4 (ND4) protein lacking 321 residues (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by comprehensive sequence analysis data presented in the manuscript and referenced figures.

claim: The w47 mutation is present at the same abundance as the uaDf5 deletion mutation (~75% of total mtDNA).
source: While this raised the possibility of two complementing mtDNA genomes, we found that the w47 mutation is present at the same abundance as the uaDf5 deletion mutation (~75% of total mtDNA, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) rather than that of the wildtype mtDNA, strongly suggesting that it resides on the same mtDNA genome.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data presented in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: ND4 is an essential transmembrane subunit within complex I of the mitochondrial respiratory chain.
source: ND4 is an essential transmembrane subunit within complex I of the mitochondrial respiratory chain (MRC), which drives NADH-oxidation-dependent transport of protons across the inner mitochondrial membrane (Lemire, 2005; van der Bliek et al., 2017; Sousa et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: Animals harboring mtDNAuaDf5 show a significant reduction in brood size compared to wildtype (WT 304 ± 4.8; uaDf5 201 ± 8.6 embryos laid, p < 0.001).
source: However, we found that uaDf5-bearing animals displayed a significant reduction in brood size (WT 304 ± 4.8; uaDf5 201 ± 8.6 embryos laid, p < 0.001) (Figure 1B)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis presented in Figure 1B.

claim: Animals harboring mtDNAuaDf5 show a significant increase in embryonic lethality compared to wildtype (WT 1.4 ± 0.2%; uaDf5 4.2 ± 0.7%, p < 0.001).
source: and a significant increase in embryonic lethality (WT 1.4 ± 0.2%; uaDf5 4.2 ± 0.7%, p < 0.001) (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis presented in Figure 1C.

claim: uaDf5 animals are slow-growing, evident in both the number of hours to reach gravidity (WT 63 ± 0.8; uaDf5 76 ± 1.4 hr at 20°C, p < 0.001).
source: Additionally, uaDf5 animals are slow-growing, evident in both the number of hours to reach gravidity (WT 63 ± 0.8; uaDf5 76 ± 1.4 hr at 20°C, p < 0.001) (Figure 1D)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data with statistical analysis presented in Figure 1D.

claim: Lifespan was not substantially affected by mtDNAuaDf5 (WT 14 ± 0.4; uaDf5 15 ± 0.5 days).
source: In contrast, however, we were surprised to find that lifespan was not substantially affected (WT 14 ± 0.4; uaDf5 15 ± 0.5 days) (Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The steady-state fractional abundance of uaDf5 in populations of 200 day 1 adults is highly reproducible across four separate trials.
source: In a wildtype genetic background, we found that the steady-state fractional abundance of uaDf5 in populations of 200 day 1 adults (first day of adulthood) is highly reproducible across four separate trials, demonstrating the reliability and robustness of the assay.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data showing reproducibility across multiple trials.

claim: mtDNAuaDf5 constitutes the major molar fraction of mtDNA in the uaDf5-bearing strain by a nearly 3:1 ratio.
source: Our analyses confirmed that mtDNAuaDf5 constitutes the major molar fraction of mtDNA in the uaDf5-bearing strain by a nearly 3:1 ratio (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: CED-3 in C. elegans is the major executioner caspase in the canonical PCD pathway.
source: CED-3 in C. elegans is the major executioner caspase in the canonical PCD pathway (Conradt et al., 2016; Gartner et al., 2008; Cohen, 1997) and is required for virtually all PCD both in the germline and the soma (Figure 2—figure supplement 2 adapted from Figure 2 in Conradt et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: Two ced-3 mutations (n717 and n1286) that strongly block PCD showed a significant increase in the ratio of defective to normal mtDNA from a molar ratio of 2.7:1 for ced-3(+) to 3.4:1 for ced-3(n717) and 4.6:1 for ced-3(n1286).
source: We found that two ced-3 mutations that strongly block PCD (Shaham et al., 1999) showed a significant increase in the ratio of defective to normal mtDNA from a molar ratio of 2.7:1 for ced-3(+) to 3.4:1 for ced-3(n717) and 4.6:1 for ced-3(n1286) (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data with citation to Shaham et al., 1999, and presented in Figure 2A.

claim: The increase in relative abundance of mtDNAuaDf5 in ced-3(−) mutant strains is attributable to an increase in mtDNAuaDf5 and not to a decrease in wildtype mtDNAWT.
source: This effect is attributable to an increase in mtDNAuaDf5 in the PCD-deficient strains and not to a decrease in wildtype mtDNAWT. Rather, we observe an increase in the abundance of mtDNAWT in ced-3(−) mutant strains relative to ced-3(+) (1.45 × 1 05) ranging from a statistically insignificant 1.1-fold increase (1.67 × 105, p = 0.302) in ced-3(n717) to 2.2-fold increase (3.2 × 105, p = 0.0262) in ced-3(n1286) (Figure 2A, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2A and Supplementary file 2.

claim: The ced-3(−) mutations n717 and n1286 both localize to the p15 domain of the protease portion of CED-3.
source: These ced-3(−) mutations both localize to the p15 domain of the protease portion of CED-3 (Figure 2—figure supplement 3), consistent with abolition of caspase activity.
evidence: The claim is supported by reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 3 showing mutation locations.

claim: Removing CSP-1 in the csp-1(tm917) knockout mutant results in a significant increase in mtDNAuaDf5 abundance to a molar ratio of 3.9:1.
source: We found that removing CSP-1 in the csp-1(tm917) knockout mutant results in a significant increase in mtDNAuaDf5 abundance to a molar ratio of 3.9:1 (Figure 2A, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2A and Supplementary file 2.

claim: The csp-1(tm917) mutation enhances the effect of the ced-3(n717) mutation, increasing the mtDNAuaDf5:mtDNAWT molar ratio from 3.5:1 to 4.7:1.
source: Further, we found that this mutation enhances the effect of the ced-3(n717) mutation, increasing the mtDNAuaDf5:mtDNAWT molar ratio from 3.5:1 to 4.7:1 (Figure 2A, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2A and Supplementary file 2.

claim: Two ced-13 alleles (sv32 and tm536) result in a very substantial increase in the mtDNAuaDf5:mtDNAWT molar ratio (sv32: 4.2:1 and tm536: 5.1:1).
source: Consistent with a requirement for PCD in purifying selection, we found that two ced-13 alleles result in a very substantial increase in the mtDNAuaDf5:mtDNAWT molar ratio (sv32: 4.2:1 and tm536: 5.1:1) (Figure 2A, Supplementary file 2)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2A and Supplementary file 2.

claim: CED-13 is a BH3-only domain protein that acts specifically in the germline to activate PCD.
source: We sought to further investigate a potential role for PCD in mtDNA purifying selection by evaluating the requirement for the pro-apoptotic factor CED-13, a BH3-only domain protein that acts specifically in the germline to activate PCD (Conradt et al., 2016; King et al., 2019; Schumacher et al., 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: The ced-9(n1950gf) gain-of-function allele blocks the interaction of EGL-1 with CED-9 at the mitochondria and results in elimination of PCD in the soma but not the germline.
source: n1950, a gain-of-function allele of ced-9 that blocks the interaction of EGL-1 with CED-9 at the mitochondria, results in elimination of PCD in the soma but not the germline (Conradt et al., 2016; Gumienny et al., 1999; Gartner et al., 2008; Fairlie et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: The mtDNAuaDf5:mtDNAWT molar ratio was not increased in ced-9(n1950gf) mutants (2.2:1).
source: Consistent with the lack of effect of ced-9(n1950gf) on germline PCD, we found that the mtDNAuaDf5:mtDNAWT molar ratio was not increased in ced-9(n1950gf) mutants (2.2:1) (Figure 2B, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2B and Supplementary file 2.

claim: Single or double mutations of several genes that promote engulfment of cell corpses result in elevated mtDNAuaDf5:mtDNAWT molar ratios, ranging from 3.5:1 to 5.2:1.
source: Further supporting a role for PCD in purifying selection, we found that single or double mutations of several genes that promote engulfment of cell corpses result in elevated mtDNAuaDf5:mtDNAWT molar ratios, ranging from 3.5:1 to 5.2:1 (4.1:1 for ced-1(e1735), 4.5:1 for ced-2(e1752), 5.2:1 for the ced-1(e1735); ced-2(e1752) double mutant, 3.6:1 for ced-10(n1993), and 4.8:1 for ced-10(n3246); Figure 2A, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2A and Supplementary file 2.

claim: A loss-of-function mutation in csp-2 (tm3077), which elevates germline PCD, did not alter the mtDNAuaDf5:mtDNAWT molar ratio (2.9:1).
source: We found that a loss-of-function mutation in csp-2, which elevates germline PCD, did not alter the mtDNAuaDf5:mtDNAWT molar ratio (2.9:1 for the csp-2(tm3077) knockout mutation) (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2B.

claim: The ced-3(n718) allele lowers, rather than elevates, the abundance of mtDNAuaDf5 (mtDNAuaDf5:mtDNAWT molar ratio of 1.8:1).
source: First, we found that the ced-3(n718) allele lowers, rather than elevates, the abundance of mtDNAuaDf5 (mtDNAuaDf5:mtDNAWT molar ratio of 1.8:1, Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2C.

claim: The n718 mutation changes a residue in the caspase activation and recruitment domain (CARD), located within the prodomain of the CED-3 zymogen.
source: In contrast, the n718 mutation changes a residue in the caspase activation and recruitment domain (CARD), located within the prodomain of the CED-3 zymogen, which is removed upon caspase activation and affects its activation by CED-4 (Figure 2—figure supplement 3; Huang et al., 2013; Shaham et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations and reference to Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claim: Eliminating the function of CED-4 did not result in a marked increase in the relative abundance of mtDNAuaDf5.
source: Consistent with the effect of the ced-3(n718) mutation, we found that eliminating the function of the pro-apoptotic regulator CED-4, the C. elegans ortholog of mammalian Apaf1 and the upstream activator of CED-3 in the canonical PCD pathway (Fairlie et al., 2006; Yang et al., 1998), did not result in a marked increase in the relative abundance of mtDNAuaDf5. That is, while the mtDNAuaDf5:mtDNAWT molar ratio increased to 3.1:1 in the ced-4(n1894) mutant, the effect was not statistically significant. Moreover, the canonical allele ced-4(n1162) allele similarly showed no elevation in mtDNAuaDf5 (molar ratio = 2.6:1; Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2B and citations.

claim: The significant decrease in brood size observed in uaDf5-bearing animals with a wildtype nuclear background is partially suppressed by both ced-3(−) and ced-13(−) mutations.
source: Specifically, we found that the significant decrease in brood size that we observed in uaDf5-bearing animals with a wildtype nuclear background is partially suppressed by both ced-3(−) and ced-13(−) mutations, which prevent PCD (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 4A)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 4A.

claim: Lifespan is unaltered in PCD mutants even when the levels of mtDNAuaDf5 are nearly doubled.
source: Our findings further underscore the observation that accumulation of defective mtDNA in those animals that do survive does not affect longevity, as we found that lifespan is unaltered in these PCD mutants even when the levels of mtDNAuaDf5 are nearly doubled (Figure 2—figure supplement 4B, C).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 2—figure supplement 4B, C.

claim: Analysis of the abundance of mtDNAuaDf5 revealed a progressive increase throughout gravidity and post-reproductive aging, with the mtDNAuaDf5:mtDNAWT molar ratio increasing from 2.9:1 to 5.5:1.
source: Analysis of the abundance of mtDNAuaDf5 revealed a progressive increase throughout gravidity and post-reproductive aging, with the mtDNAuaDf5:mtDNAWT molar ratio increasing from 2.9:1 to 5.5:1 (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: glp-4(bn2) animals at the non-permissive temperature showed a slight decrease in the defective mtDNA from day 1 to 4 of adulthood (2.2:1 at day 1, dropping to 2:1 at day 4, for an overall decrease of 6.3%).
source: In contrast to the increased mtDNAuaDf5 abundance with age seen at permissive temperature (mtDNAuaDf5:mtDNAWT of 1.8:1 at day 1, rising to 2.6:1 at day 4, for an overall increase by 48%), we found that glp-4(bn2) animals at the non-permissive temperature showed a slight decrease in the defective mtDNA from day 1 to 4 of adulthood (2.2:1 at day 1, dropping to 2:1 at day 4, for an overall decrease of 6.3%) (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3B.

claim: Day 10 glp-4(bn2) adults grown at the restrictive temperature showed a marked increase in the mtDNAuaDf5:mtDNAWT molar ratio compared to day 1 adults even in the absence of a germline (day 10 glp-4(bn2) molar ratio of 3.4:1, a 57% increase from day 1 levels).
source: We found that mtDNAuaDf5 does eventually appear to accumulate in somatic cells with age, as day 10 adults grown at the restrictive temperature showed a marked increase in the mtDNAuaDf5:mtDNAWT molar ratio compared to day 1 adults even in the absence of a germline (day 10 glp-4(bn2) molar ratio of 3.4:1, a 57% increase from day 1 levels) (Figure 3B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3B.

claim: The abundance of mtDNAuaDf5 is reduced during transmission between mother and offspring (average decrease ranging from 6% to 13%).
source: This analysis led to two key observations: (1) the abundance of mtDNAuaDf5 is reduced during transmission between mother and offspring (average decrease ranging from 6% to 13%), presumably as a result of purifying selection
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data analysis.

claim: The abundance of the defective mtDNA in the offspring correlates with the age of the mothers: the progeny of older mothers contain a markedly higher mtDNAuaDf5:mtDNAWT molar ratio (4.2:1) than that of younger mothers (2.6:1).
source: and (2) the abundance of the defective mtDNA in the offspring correlates with the age of the mothers: the progeny of older mothers contain a markedly higher mtDNAuaDf5:mtDNAWT molar ratio (4.2:1) than that of younger mothers (2.6:1) (Figure 3C, D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 3C, D.

claim: Two mutant alleles of daf-2 (e1391 and e1370) that affect the kinase domain and which reduce rates of aging and increase lifespan, result in dramatically decreased mtDNAuaDf5:mtDNAWT molar ratios from 2.8:1 to as low as 0.3:1 (0.3:1 for daf-2(e1391); 0.8:1 for daf-2(e1370)).
source: We found that two mutant alleles of daf-2 that affect the kinase domain and which reduce rates of aging and increase lifespan, result in dramatically decreased mtDNAuaDf5:mtDNAWT molar ratios from 2.8:1 to as low as 0.3:1 (0.3:1 for daf-2(e1391); 0.8:1 for daf-2(e1370); Figure 4A; see Supplementary file 3 for a list of lifespan mutants used in the analyses).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4A.

claim: Two daf-16 mutants (mu86 and mgDf50) result in slightly increased, albeit not statistically significant, mtDNAuaDf5:mtDNAWT molar ratios (3.3:1 for daf-16(mu86); 3.5:1 for daf-16(mgDf50)).
source: We found that eliminating DAF-16 in two daf-16 mutants results in slightly increased, albeit not statistically significant, mtDNAuaDf5:mtDNAWT molar ratios (3.3:1 for daf-16(mu86); 3.5:1 for daf-16(mgDf50)) (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4B.

claim: Removal of DAF-16 in the daf-16(mu86) mutant suppressed the decreased mtDNAuaDf5:mtDNAWT molar ratios observed in two daf-2 mutants, from 0.3:1 for daf-2(e1391) to 1:1 for daf-16(mu86); daf-2(e1391) and from 0.6:1 for daf-2(e1370) to 1.8:1 for daf-16(mu86); daf-2(e1370).
source: Further, we found that removal of DAF-16 in the daf-16(mu86) mutant suppressed the decreased mtDNAuaDf5:mtDNAWT molar ratios observed in two daf-2 mutants, from 0.3:1 for daf-2(e1391) to 1:1 for daf-16(mu86); daf-2(e1391) and from 0.6:1 for daf-2(e1370) to 1.8:1 for daf-16(mu86); daf-2(e1370), consistent with observations reported in a recent study (Kirby and Patel, 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and a citation to Kirby and Patel, 2021.

claim: Two mutations that reduce lifespan by eliminating the function of AAK-2 result in elevated mtDNAuaDf5:mtDNAWT molar ratios as high as 4.4:1 compared to 2.8:1 in wildtype animals (3.8:1 for aak-2(ok524) and 4.4:1 for aak-2(gt33)).
source: We found, conversely, that two mutations that reduce lifespan by eliminating the function of AAK-2 (AMP activated kinase-2), a conserved factor acting in the IIS pathway (Murphy and Hu, 2013; Haroon et al., 2018), result in elevated mtDNAuaDf5:mtDNAWT molar ratios as high as 4.4:1 compared to 2.8:1 in wildtype animals (3.8:1 for aak-2(ok524) and 4.4:1 for aak-2(gt33)) (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4B and citations.

claim: Long-lived clk-1(qm30) mutants showed a greatly diminished mtDNAuaDf5:mtDNAWT molar ratio of 0.3:1.
source: As with long-lived daf-2 mutants, we found that long-lived clk-1(qm30) mutants showed a greatly diminished mtDNAuaDf5:mtDNAWT molar ratio of 0.3:1 (Figure 4A)
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4A.

claim: mtDNAuaDf5 was completely eliminated in daf-2(e1391) clk-1(qm30) double mutants.
source: Indeed, we found that mtDNAuaDf5 was completely eliminated in daf-2(e1391) clk-1(qm30) double mutants, revealing a strongly synergistic effect between the two age-determining systems (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4A.

claim: Analysis of 21 different genetic backgrounds over the first 10 days of adulthood revealed that the age-dependent progressive accumulation of mtDNAuaDf5 is a consistent phenomenon.
source: Analysis of 21 different genetic backgrounds over the first 10 days of adulthood revealed that the age-dependent progressive accumulation of mtDNAuaDf5 is a consistent phenomenon (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4D.

claim: All long-lived mutants in either the IIS pathway or clk-1 accumulate mtDNAuaDf5 at a substantially slower rate as they age than do wildtype animals.
source: Comparison of long-lived mutants and wildtype using a linear regression model revealed a striking positive correlation between aging rate and age-dependent rate of accumulation of mtDNAuaDf5: all long-lived mutants in either the IIS pathway or clk-1 accumulate mtDNAuaDf5 at a substantially slower rate as they age than do wildtype animals (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 2A, B).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data and linear regression analysis presented in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A, B.

claim: The aak-2(ok524) and daf-16(mu86) single mutants and daf-16(−);daf-2(−) double mutants all showed increased rates of mtDNAuaDf5 accumulation.
source: Conversely, we analyzed six short-lived IIS pathway mutant combinations and found that the aak-2(ok524) and daf-16(mu86) single mutants and daf-16(−);daf-2(−) double mutants all showed increased rates of mtDNAuaDf5 accumulation (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 2C, D).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 2C, D.

claim: The brood size is decreased and embryonic lethality is increased in short-lived daf-16(−) mutants, but not in the long-lived clk-1(−) mutant compared to those in a wildtype nuclear background.
source: Consistent with a relationship between aging rates and accumulation of defective mtDNA, we found that the brood size is decreased and embryonic lethality is increased in short-lived daf-16(−) mutants, but not in the long-lived clk-1(−) mutant compared to those in a wildtype nuclear background (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: The offspring of day 4 adults in strains with significantly higher steady-state fractional abundance of mtDNAuaDf5 showed significantly greater rates of reduction of the defective mtDNA ranging from 24% reduction in ced-10(n1993) to 17.4% in ced-13(sv32) to 14.5% in atfs-1(et15).
source: The offspring of day 4 adults in those strains ('high' strains) with significantly higher steady-state fractional abundance of mtDNAuaDf5 showed significantly greater rates of reduction of the defective mtDNA ranging from 24% reduction in ced-10(n1993) (fractional abundance of mtDNAuaDf5 of 6.5:1–2.8:1) and 17.4% in ced-13(sv32) (6.4:1–3.3:1) to 14.5% in atfs-1(et15) (5.4:1–3.3:1), compared to offspring of ('low' strain) mothers with lower steady-state fractional abundance of the mutant mtDNA (13.5% reduction in ced-3(n2454) (3.9:1–2.8:1); 12.7% in ced-4(n1162) (3.2:1–2.5:1) versus only 3.2% in WT (4.7:1–4.2:1)).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data analysis.

claim: There is a strong correlation (r2 = 0.61, p < 0.001) between the steady-state level of mtDNAuaDf5 in mothers and the capacity for its removal between mother and progeny during day 4 of adulthood.
source: Indeed, we found a strong correlation (r2 = 0.61, p < 0.001) between the steady-state level of mtDNAuaDf5 in mothers and the capacity for its removal between mother and progeny during day 4 of adulthood (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical correlation analysis presented in Figure 5B.

claim: Regulators of germline PCD are required for effective removal of deleterious mtDNA from the germline.
source: We report eight major findings: (1) regulators of germline PCD are required for effective removal of deleterious mtDNA from the germline
evidence: This is a summary claim stated in the Discussion section, supported by the experimental findings presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The cell death machinery functions in a non-canonical caspase-dependent but CED-4-independent cell death pathway to mediate mitochondrial purifying selection.
source: (2) the cell death machinery functions in a non-canonical caspase-dependent but CED-4-independent cell death pathway to mediate mitochondrial purifying selection
evidence: This is a summary claim stated in the Discussion section, supported by the experimental findings presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The CSP-1 caspase has as strong of an effect on mitochondrial purifying selection as the major PCD regulator CED-3.
source: (3) the CSP-1 caspase has as strong of an effect on mitochondrial purifying selection as the major PCD regulator CED-3
evidence: This is a summary claim stated in the Discussion section, supported by the experimental findings presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: mtDNAuaDf5 progressively accumulates in the germline as adults age.
source: (4) mtDNAuaDf5 progressively accumulates in the germline as adults age
evidence: This is a summary claim stated in the Discussion section, supported by the experimental findings presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Age-dependent accumulation of mtDNAuaDf5 is transmitted to progeny; however, the burden of the defective mtDNA is lower in offspring than mothers suggesting intergenerational purifying selection.
source: (5) this age-dependent accumulation of mtDNAuaDf5 is transmitted to progeny; however, the burden of the defective mtDNA is lower in offspring than mothers suggesting intergenerational purifying selection
evidence: This is a summary claim stated in the Discussion section, supported by the experimental findings presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Two separate aging pathways, the IIS and CLK-1 pathways, act synergistically to regulate mtDNAuaDf5 levels; longer-lived mutants show reduced levels of the defective mtDNA while shorter-lived mutants show increased levels compared to otherwise wildtype animals.
source: (6) two separate aging pathways, the IIS and CLK-1 pathways, act synergistically to regulate mtDNAuaDf5 levels; longer-lived mutants show reduced levels of the defective mtDNA while shorter-lived mutants show increased levels compared to otherwise wildtype animals
evidence: This is a summary claim stated in the Discussion section, supported by the experimental findings presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The rate of mtDNAuaDf5 accumulation is inversely correlated with lifespan in aging mutants.
source: (7) the rate of mtDNAuaDf5 accumulation is inversely correlated with lifespan in aging mutants
evidence: This is a summary claim stated in the Discussion section, supported by the experimental findings presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Intergenerational removal of mtDNAuaDf5 occurs more effectively during transmission from older mothers with high burden of the defective mtDNA.
source: (8) intergenerational removal of mtDNAuaDf5 occurs more effectively during transmission from older mothers with high burden of the defective mtDNA.
evidence: This is a summary claim stated in the Discussion section, supported by the experimental findings presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: During germline development in C. elegans, as many as 95% of nuclei destined to become potential oocytes are eliminated by PCD.
source: During germline development in C. elegans, as many as 95% of nuclei destined to become potential oocytes are eliminated by PCD (Gumienny et al., 1999; Baum et al., 2005; Jaramillo-Lambert et al., 2007; Gartner et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: Mitochondrial diseases affect mitochondrial functions in up to 1 in 4300 people.
source: Mitochondrial diseases are a group of conditions that affect mitochondrial functions in up to 1 in 4300 people (Ng and Turnbull, 2016; Chinnery, 2015; Gorman et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: Mitochondrial diseases most commonly present as dysfunction in the tissues or organs with the most intensive energy demands, most commonly in muscle and the nervous system.
source: Generally, these diseases present as dysfunction in the tissues or organs with the most intensive energy demands, most commonly in muscle and the nervous system (Ghaoui and Sue, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ghaoui and Sue, 2018.

claim: The progressive advancement of the diseased state resulting from age-dependent accumulation of mutant mtDNA is a common trait among mitochondrial diseases.
source: The progressive advancement of the diseased state resulting from age-dependent accumulation of mutant mtDNA is a common trait among mitochondrial diseases (Dhillon and Fenech, 2014; Park and Larsson, 2011; Burté et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: There are currently no pharmacological treatments for mitochondrial diseases.
source: As there are currently no pharmacological treatments for mitochondrial diseases, it is of great importance to uncover the cellular processes that underlie the regulation of mtDNA quality control.
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: mtDNAs show high mutation rates.
source: mtDNAs show high mutation rates (Brown et al., 1979; Konrad et al., 2017; Denver et al., 2000)
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: Processes that regulate mtDNA quality control include mitochondrial fission/fusion dynamics and mitophagy.
source: Processes that regulate mtDNA quality control include mitochondrial fission/fusion dynamics and mitophagy (Burté et al., 2015; Twig and Shirihai, 2011; Busch et al., 2014; Ni et al., 2015; Ashrafi and Schwarz, 2013; Youle and Narendra, 2011; Tilokani et al., 2018)
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to established literature.

claim: The mitochondrial unfolded protein response (UPRMT) is a process that regulates mtDNA quality control.
source: and the mitochondrial unfolded protein response (UPRMT; Hernando-Rodríguez and Artal-Sanz, 2018; Rolland et al., 2019; Münch, 2018; Callegari and Dennerlein, 2018; Gitschlag et al., 2016; Nargund et al., 2012; Lin et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to established literature.
